q: In the Seneca I General Specifications, what is the minimum controllable single-engine speed (Vmc)?
a: 80 MPH
d: 76 MPH
90 MPH
105 MPH
why: POH 1-1 lists 80 MPH at both 4,000 and 4,200 lb; it is the red radial line on the airspeed indicator. 76 MPH is a gear-down, flaps-up stall speed, 90 MPH is Vx and 105 MPH is Vyse.

q: Per the Seneca I specifications, what are the best rate-of-climb speed (Vy) and the best single-engine rate-of-climb speed (Vyse)?
a: Both are 105 MPH (91.5 kt)
d: Vy 105 MPH (91.5 kt); Vyse 90 MPH (78 kt)
Vy 120 MPH; Vyse 105 MPH (91.5 kt)
Both are 90 MPH (78 kt)
why: POH 1-1 gives 105 MPH (91.5 kt) for both, at either weight. 90 MPH is Vx, and 120 MPH is the en route climb speed suggested in Section 6.

q: What best angle-of-climb speed (Vx) does the Seneca I POH list?
a: 90 MPH
d: 80 MPH
85 MPH
105 MPH
why: POH 1-1 lists Vx as 90 MPH (78 kt). 80 MPH is Vmc, 85 MPH is the 50-ft speed in the flaps-up short-field takeoff, and 105 MPH is Vy.

q: POH 1-1 also lists stall speeds at the 4,000-lb maximum landing weight. Power off, what are they with gear and flaps down, and with gear down, flaps up?
a: 67 MPH flaps down; 73 MPH flaps up
d: 69 MPH flaps down; 76 MPH flaps up
67 MPH flaps down; 76 MPH flaps up
63 MPH flaps down; 69 MPH flaps up
why: POH 1-1 at 4,000 lb: 67 MPH (58 kt) gear and flaps down, 73 MPH (63.5 kt) gear down and flaps up. 69 and 76 MPH are the 4,200-lb figures; stall speed falls as weight decreases.

q: At 4,200 lb, power off, gear down and flaps up, what stall speed does POH 1-1 list?
a: 76 MPH (66 kt)
d: 69 MPH (60 kt)
67 MPH (58 kt)
why: 76 MPH at 4,200 lb (73 MPH at 4,000 lb). It matches the bottom of the green arc; 69 MPH, the full-flap stall at 4,200 lb, is the bottom of the white arc.

q: At max gross weight (4,200 lb), sea level, standard day, what single-engine rate of climb does the POH spec table give?
a: 190 fpm
d: 230 fpm
50 fpm
why: POH 1-1: 190 fpm at 4,200 lb (230 fpm at 4,000 lb), against 1,360 fpm with both engines. Losing an engine costs well over 80% of the climb performance.

q: What is the Seneca I single-engine service ceiling (left engine out) at 4,200 lb, per the POH specifications?
why: POH 1-1: 3,650 ft at 4,200 lb and 5,200 ft at 4,000 lb. 5,000 ft and 6,600 ft are the single-engine absolute ceilings at those weights.

q: At 4,200 lb on a standard day, the left engine fails while you are level at 4,500 ft pressure altitude. Once it is feathered and you are clean at Vyse, what climb can you expect per POH 1-1?
a: A positive climb of less than 50 fpm
d: About 190 fpm, the sea-level figure
None; you are above the absolute ceiling
About 100 fpm, the service ceiling rate
why: At 4,200 lb the single-engine service ceiling (50 fpm) is 3,650 ft and the absolute ceiling (zero climb) is 5,000 ft. At 4,500 ft you are between them, so only a small climb remains.

q: POH 1-1 short-field takeoff (flaps 25°) at 4,200 lb: what are the ground run and the distance over a 50-ft barrier?
a: 800 ft run; 1,235 ft over 50 ft
d: 750 ft run; 1,140 ft over 50 ft
705 ft run; 1,335 ft over 50 ft
1,235 ft run; 1,800 ft over 50 ft
why: 800/1,235 ft at 4,200 lb; 750/1,140 ft is the 4,000-lb figure and 705/1,335 ft is the short-field landing. Use the Section 8 charts for actual conditions.

q: What short-field landing distances (flaps down) appear in the Seneca I General Specifications?
a: 705 ft roll; 1,335 ft over a 50-ft barrier
d: 800 ft roll; 1,235 ft over a 50-ft barrier
1,335 ft roll; 2,000 ft over a 50-ft barrier
750 ft roll; 1,140 ft over a 50-ft barrier
why: POH 1-1 lists 705 ft and 1,335 ft, with a footnote that they apply only to the conditions on the Landing Distance vs Density Altitude chart. 800/1,235 and 750/1,140 are takeoff figures.

q: Planning a cruise at 75% power, what total fuel burn for both engines does POH 1-1 list, and what at 65% power?
a: 20.6 GPH at 75%; 18.3 GPH at 65%
d: 10.3 GPH at 75%; 9.2 GPH at 65%
19.2 GPH at 75%; 16.0 GPH at 65%
24.0 GPH at 75%; 20.6 GPH at 65%
why: 20.6 and 18.3 GPH are totals for both engines (roughly half each per engine). 19.2 GPH is the fuel flow gauge red line in Section 3, not a consumption figure.

q: What are the Seneca I maximum takeoff and maximum landing weights?
a: 4,200 lb takeoff; 4,000 lb landing
d: 4,200 lb for both takeoff and landing
4,570 lb takeoff; 4,342 lb landing
4,000 lb takeoff; 3,800 lb landing
why: POH 1-2 lists 4,200 lb max takeoff and 4,000 lb max landing weight; the spec-table footnote repeats both.

q: What are the maximum baggage loads for the Seneca I forward and rear compartments?
a: 100 lb forward; 100 lb rear
d: 100 lb forward; 200 lb rear
150 lb forward; 100 lb rear
200 lb forward; 200 lb rear
why: POH 1-2: 100 lb in each, with 15.3 cu ft forward and 20 cu ft rear (forward door 24 x 21 in). The loading must also keep the CG within limits.

q: Which Seneca I engine is the Lycoming LIO-360-C1E6?
a: The right engine
d: The left engine
Both; the 'L' marks the injected model
Both; the 'L' marks later serial numbers
why: POH 1-2 and 3-1: left engine IO-360-C1E6, right engine LIO-360-C1E6. The right engine is the one that turns counterclockwise, giving counter-rotation.

q: Viewed from the cockpit, which way does each Seneca I engine rotate?
a: Left clockwise; right counterclockwise
d: Left counterclockwise; right clockwise
Both clockwise
Both counterclockwise
why: POH 2-2: the left engine turns clockwise and the right counterclockwise as seen from the cockpit. This counter-rotation removes asymmetric thrust in takeoff and climb.

q: What is each Seneca I engine's rated power, and what are its operating limits?
a: 200 HP at 2,700 RPM, approved for all operations
d: 200 HP at 2,700 RPM, with a 5-minute takeoff limit
220 HP at 2,800 RPM, for takeoff only
180 HP at 2,700 RPM, for continuous use
why: POH 1-2/2-2: 200 HP at 2,700 RPM each, 400 HP total. The limitations list 2,700 RPM and 200 HP for all operations, and Section 6 says full power has no time limit.

q: How many cylinders, what displacement and what compression ratio does each Seneca I engine have?
a: Four cylinders, 361 cu in, 8.7:1
d: Four cylinders, 320 cu in, 8.5:1
Six cylinders, 361 cu in, 8.7:1
Six cylinders, 540 cu in, 7.3:1
why: POH 1-2: 361.0 cu in, 8.7:1 compression, 5.125-in bore, 4.375-in stroke, 350 lb dry weight. POH 2-2 describes them as four-cylinder, fuel-injected Lycomings.

q: How is fuel delivered to the Seneca I engines?
a: Bendix RSA-5 fuel injection metered by engine airflow
d: Marvel-Schebler float carburetors with mixture and carb heat
Timed direct cylinder injection metered by engine RPM
Bendix pressure carburetors with accelerator pumps
why: POH 2-2: each engine has a Bendix RSA-5 system that measures the engine's air consumption and uses that airflow to control fuel flow. There is no carburetor and no carb heat.

q: Is the Seneca I (PA-34-200) turbocharged?
a: No; air goes from the filter straight to the fuel servo
d: Yes; both engines have turbochargers with fixed wastegates
Yes; only the right (LIO-360) engine has a turbocharger
Yes; the turbos also feed heated air to the alternate air box
why: POH 2-3 describes induction air going from the scoop through the filter directly to the servo regulator, with no turbocharger in the path. Expect power to fall off with altitude.

q: Where does normal induction air enter each Seneca I engine?
a: A scoop on the outboard side of the lower cowl, then a filter
d: A scoop on the inboard side of the upper cowl, then a filter
The oil cooler scoops on the sides of the cowl
The dorsal fin air scoop, then a filter
why: POH 2-3: an air scoop on the outboard lower cowl feeds a filter and then the servo regulator. The side-cowl scoops feed the oil cooler (POH 2-2).

q: How does the Seneca I alternate air system work?
a: A manual valve admits unfiltered air heated by the exhaust
d: A spring door opens automatically when the filter clogs
It routes carburetor heat from a muffler shroud
A manual valve admits filtered ram air from the nose
why: POH 2-3: a valve in the air box between the filter and servo regulator, worked by the control below the power quadrant, admits air heated by the crossover exhaust tube that bypasses the filter.

q: In cruise you fly into heavy snow and manifold pressure on both engines begins to drop. What does the POH system design call for?
a: Select alternate air; heated air bypasses the iced filter
d: Apply carburetor heat on both engines
Open the cowl flaps to warm the induction air
Lean the mixtures until manifold pressure recovers
why: POH 2-3 and 6-9: snow or freezing rain can ice the air filter. Alternate air bypasses the filter and is heated by the crossover exhaust, but it is not automatic; the pilot must select it.

q: When does the POH say alternate air should NOT be used on the Seneca I?
a: During ground operation and for takeoff
d: Above 10,000 ft, where exhaust heat is too low
In visible moisture below freezing
During climb, because it overheats the cylinders
why: POH 2-3: unfiltered alternate air may carry dust on the ground, and the primary induction source should always be used for takeoff. A brief run-up check is allowed unless the air is dusty (POH 6-5).

q: How do the Seneca I cowl flaps operate?
a: Manual levers with a lock: open, intermediate, closed
d: Electric switches with an indicator: open or closed
Manual levers with infinite positions and no lock
Automatic, driven by a cylinder head thermostat
why: POH 2-2: levers below the throttle quadrant work cowl flaps on the bottom of each nacelle. Depress the lock for each selection; once released, the flap stops at the next position.

q: In a climb with the left engine's CHT rising, you want its cowl flap open. How do you move the control?
a: Depress the lock and push the left lever
d: Depress the lock and pull the left lever
Pull the left lever; no lock is used
Push the right lever; the levers are linked
why: The cowl flap placard (POH 2-3) reads PULL–CLOSE and PUSH–OPEN, with separate L and R levers. The lock must be depressed for each selection (POH 2-2).

q: Where is each Seneca I engine's oil cooler, and how is it cooled?
a: Forward of the firewall, fed by scoops on the cowl sides
d: Aft of the firewall, cooled by cabin ventilation air
Behind the spinner, fed by the main cowl nose inlet
Under the nacelle, cooled by air leaving the cowl flaps
why: POH 2-2: air picked up by scoops on the side of the cowl passes through the oil cooler on the forward side of the firewall and is ducted overboard in the lower cowling.

q: What is each Seneca I engine's oil capacity, and what minimum quantity does the POH call safe?
a: 8 quarts capacity; 2 quarts minimum safe
d: 8 quarts capacity; 4 quarts minimum safe
6 quarts capacity; 3 quarts minimum safe
12 quarts capacity; 8 quarts minimum safe
why: POH 1-2 and 9-7: 8 quarts each, with a minimum safe quantity of 2 quarts. The Section 6 preflight looks for six to eight quarts before flight.

q: Operating in summer with temperatures consistently above 90°F, which oil grade does the POH call for?
a: SAE 50
d: SAE 40
SAE 30
SAE 20
why: POH 9-7: SAE 50 above 60°F, SAE 40 from 30 to 90°F, SAE 30 from 0 to 70°F, SAE 20 below 10°F. Above 90°F only SAE 50 applies.

q: What are the Seneca I normal (green arc) oil pressure and oil temperature ranges?
why: POH 3-1: oil pressure green 60–90 PSI (yellow 25–60, red line max 90); oil temperature green 75–245°F with a 245°F red line. 14–35 PSI is fuel pressure; 200–475°F is CHT.

q: During the Seneca I run-up magneto check, what are the normal drop, maximum drop and maximum differential?
a: 100 RPM normal; 175 RPM max; 50 RPM differential
d: 125 RPM normal; 175 RPM max; 50 RPM differential
100 RPM normal; 150 RPM max; 75 RPM differential
50 RPM normal; 125 RPM max; 50 RPM differential
why: POH 6-5 lists normal drop 100 RPM, maximum drop 175 RPM and maximum differential 50 RPM; the school run-up checklist uses the same numbers.

q: In a long climb, CHT and oil temperature are both nearing their limits. Which actions does the POH recommend?
a: Enrich the mixture, open the cowl flaps, reduce power
d: Lean the mixture, close the cowl flaps, raise the nose
Select alternate air and reduce propeller RPM only
Turn on the electric fuel pumps and lean the mixture
why: POH 6-8: reduce high CHT by enriching the mixture, opening cowl flaps, reducing power, or a combination. Keep CHT below 475°F; a 120 MPH en route climb also helps cooling.

q: Describe the Seneca I propellers.
a: Hartzell constant-speed, full-feathering, oil and nitrogen
d: Hartzell constant-speed, non-feathering, governor oil pressure only
McCauley constant-speed, full-feathering, oil and springs
Hartzell fixed-pitch, counter-rotating, 76-in diameter
why: POH 2-4: constant-speed, controllable-pitch, full-feathering Hartzell propellers operated by oil and nitrogen pressure. Diameter is 76 in (POH 1-2); the limitations allow 74 to 76 in (POH 3-1).

q: In the Seneca I propeller, what does increasing governor oil pressure do to the blades?
a: Moves them toward low pitch / high RPM (unfeather)
d: Moves them toward high pitch / low RPM (feather)
Locks them against the low-pitch stop
Nothing until engine RPM exceeds 800
why: POH 2-4: oil pressure, supplied by an engine-mounted governor through the prop shaft, drives the prop toward high RPM/unfeather; nitrogen drives it toward low RPM/feather.

q: What two jobs does the nitrogen charge in the Seneca I propeller dome do?
a: Drives blades toward feather and guards against overspeed
d: Drives blades toward high RPM and assists unfeathering in flight
Stores oil under pressure to unfeather the prop without the starter
Cools the hub and damps blade vibration at high RPM
why: POH 2-4: nitrogen pressure sends the prop toward low RPM/feather and keeps it from overspeeding. Dry compressed air may be used instead; the charge pressure placard is on the dome and in the spinner.

q: During the 1,500-RPM feather check, RPM takes about 6 seconds to fall to 1,000 RPM. What might this indicate?
a: Low dome pressure; risk of overspeed or lost feathering
d: Normal; up to 6 seconds is allowed
A weak magneto on that engine
High dome pressure; risk of slow unfeathering
why: POH 6-5: RPM should drop to 1,000 in 1–3 seconds. Longer suggests excessively low dome pressure, with danger of propeller overspeed or loss of feathering capability.

q: How do you feather a Seneca I propeller?
a: Pull the prop lever fully aft through the low-RPM detent
d: Pull the prop lever back to the low-RPM detent and hold it there
Press the feather button for that engine, then pull the mixture
Pull the prop lever fully aft once the RPM is below 800
why: POH 2-4: move the control fully aft through the low-RPM detent into the feather position. It must be done while the engine is still turning above 800 RPM.

q: About how long does a Seneca I propeller take to feather?
a: About 6 seconds
d: About 1–3 seconds
About 10–12 seconds
About 30 seconds
why: POH 2-4: feathering takes approximately six seconds. The 1–3 seconds figure is the run-up feather check drop to 1,000 RPM.

q: How is a Seneca I propeller unfeathered in flight?
a: Prop lever forward, then engage the starter until it windmills
d: Prop lever forward; the unfeathering accumulator does the rest
Prop lever forward, then dive steeply until it windmills
Throttle full and mixture rich, then pull the prop lever aft
why: POH 2-4: move the propeller control ahead and engage the starter until the propeller is windmilling. The POH describes no unfeathering accumulator.

q: What does the Seneca I's centrifugal feathering lock do?
a: Prevents feathering whenever engine speed is below 800 RPM
d: Prevents unfeathering whenever engine speed is above 800 RPM
Locks the blades in feather while on the ground
Prevents feathering whenever RPM is above 2,000
why: POH 2-4: the centrifugally operated lock makes feathering impossible below 800 RPM, so the propellers don't feather during a normal engine shutdown.

q: An engine is losing oil pressure and its RPM is decaying. You decide to feather it to save the engine. What is the key timing concern?
a: Feather before RPM drops below 800, or the lock prevents it
d: Wait until RPM is below 800 so the lock releases
Feather only after the prop stops windmilling
Feather only after slowing to Vmc
why: POH 2-4: because feathering is impossible below 800 RPM, a pilot feathering to save an engine must move the control to feather before RPM falls below 800.

q: Loss of the dome air charge causes a propeller overspeed. Per the POH, what can you expect, and what is the first step?
a: The prop won't feather; close the throttle
d: The prop feathers itself; secure the engine
The prop won't feather; pull the mixture
The governor recovers; push the prop lever forward
why: POH 3-18: in an overspeed the propeller will not feather. Close the throttle, slow to best rate-of-climb speed, pull the prop to low RPM, then slowly add throttle until the governor engages.

q: According to the Seneca I POH, what does counter-rotation of the propellers accomplish?
a: Balanced thrust; no 'critical engine' in single-engine flight
d: Makes the right engine the critical engine instead of the left
Lowers Vmc below the power-off stall speed in all conditions
Removes the need for rudder or rudder trim on one engine
why: POH 2-2/2-4: counter-rotation eliminates asymmetric thrust in takeoff and climb and the 'critical engine' factor. Vmc (80 MPH) still applies, and the rudder trim tab exists for single-engine flight.

q: What powers the Seneca I landing gear for normal retraction and extension?
a: A reversible, electrically powered hydraulic pump
d: An engine-driven hydraulic pump on the left engine
A direct electric motor and screw jack
An engine-driven pump with an electric backup
why: POH 2-4: hydraulic pressure comes from an electrically powered reversible pump. Pressure in one direction retracts the gear; in the other it extends it.

q: Where is the Seneca I gear selector, and how is it operated?
a: Left of the quadrant; pull the wheel knob out, then move it
d: Right of the quadrant; push the wheel knob in, then move it
On the floor console; lift the lever over a detent
Left of the quadrant; move it with no pull-out needed
why: POH 2-4: the two-position switch with a wheel-shaped knob is on the panel to the left of the control quadrant and must be pulled out before it can move to UP or DOWN.

q: Just after selecting gear UP you decide you want it down again. The gear is in transit with the pump running. What does the POH caution?
a: Don't reverse until travel completes; it can harm the pump
d: Reverse immediately; the pump stops and reverses automatically
Pull the emergency knob instead of reversing the selector
Cycle the master switch off and on, then select DOWN
why: POH 2-4: moving the selector the opposite way before the gear reaches its travel limit is inadvisable because the sudden reversal may harm the electric pump. A full cycle takes 6–7 seconds.

q: How long does normal Seneca I gear retraction or extension take?
a: 6 to 7 seconds
d: 3 to 4 seconds
10 to 12 seconds
About 20 seconds
why: POH 2-4: retraction or extension normally takes six to seven seconds.

q: What holds the Seneca I landing gear in the retracted position?
a: Hydraulic pressure only; there are no mechanical uplocks
d: Mechanical uplock hooks, released by hydraulic pressure
Over-center links held in place by bungee springs
Electric solenoid uplocks wired to the up-limit switches
why: POH 2-5: the gear is held up by hydraulic pressure, and POH 6-9 states there are no mechanical uplocks. Lose the pressure and the gear free-falls.

q: In cruise, a leak drains the landing gear hydraulic pressure. What will the gear do?
a: Extend by gravity, helped by airloads and springs
d: Stay up, held by its mechanical uplock hooks
Stay up until the emergency extension knob is pulled
Extend only the nose gear, while the mains stay retracted
why: POH 2-5: if the system leaks or pressure is relieved, gravity extends the gear, with aerodynamic loads and springs assisting extension and locking.

q: How is the Seneca I landing gear held locked in the down position?
a: Downlock hooks kept engaged by springs
d: Hydraulic pressure trapped by a check valve
Over-center drag links with no springs
Electric solenoids energized by the squat switch
why: POH 2-5: when all three gear are down the downlock hooks engage, and a spring keeps force on each hook until hydraulic pressure releases it for retraction.

q: What does the Seneca I emergency gear extension knob do, and where is it?
a: Releases hydraulic pressure; near panel center, under a guard
d: Runs a backup electric pump; near panel center, under a guard
Releases the mechanical uplock hooks; on the floor console
Engages a hand crank for the gear; below the pilot's seat
why: POH 2-5: pulling the knob releases the hydraulic pressure holding the gear up so it can free-fall. A guard over the knob (the clip in POH 3-14) prevents inadvertent extension.

q: Before pulling the emergency gear extension knob, where should the gear selector be, and why?
a: DOWN, so the pump doesn't try to raise the gear
d: UP, so the downlock hooks are not loaded during free-fall
Left where it is, to avoid a sudden reversal harming the pump
UP, so the pump can't run during free-fall
why: POH 2-5 advises placing the selector DOWN first to prevent the pump from trying to raise the gear. The manual extension checklist (POH 3-14) does the same.

q: In the POH manual landing gear extension procedure, what is the maximum airspeed?
a: 100 MPH
d: 125 MPH
150 MPH
105 MPH
why: POH 3-14: reduce power so airspeed does not exceed 100 MPH, select gear DOWN, pull the emergency knob, check three green and leave the knob out. 150 MPH is the normal extension limit.

q: After lowering the gear with the emergency knob because of a real malfunction, what does the POH require?
a: Leave the knob out until the airplane is jacked and checked
d: Push the knob in after landing to restore pressure
Push the knob in once three greens show
Recycle the gear on the next flight to test it
why: POH 2-5: leave the control out until the airplane is on jacks and the gear hydraulic and electrical systems are checked. On training flights with no apparent malfunction, it may be pushed back in.

q: What cockpit and external indications show the Seneca I gear position?
a: Three green, a red light, and a mirror on the left nacelle
d: Three green and a red light, with no external aid
Three green and a mechanical floor indicator
Three green, a red light, and a mirror on the right nacelle
why: POH 2-5: three green = down and locked; red = not fully up or fully down; a convex mirror on the left engine nacelle lets the pilot confirm the nose gear.

q: Daytime approach: you select gear DOWN and hear the pump stop, but see no green lights. What should you check first?
a: The navigation light switch; it dims the gear lights
d: The emergency extension knob; it may be partly out
The gear pump circuit breaker; it may have tripped
The left-main squat switch; it may be stuck open
why: POH 2-5: the gear lights dim automatically when the nav lights are on and are hard to see in daylight. The POH says this is the first thing to check if the greens aren't seen.

q: With gear DOWN selected, one green light stays dark. Per the POH, which three conditions could cause it?
a: Gear not locked, bulb burned out, or indicating fault
d: Gear not locked, low hydraulic fluid, or squat switch open
Bulb burned out, pump failure, or nav lights off
Gear not locked, low battery, or throttle switch fault
why: POH 2-5 lists these three possibilities for each green light that fails to come on after DOWN is selected. For the nose gear, the mirror on the left nacelle gives an independent check.

q: During a Vmc demo with the gear up, you bring one throttle back to idle and a horn sounds steadily. What is it most likely telling you?
a: Gear up with manifold pressure below 14 in on one engine
d: Stall warning from the inboard stall detector
Gear selector UP with the squat switch open
Overspeed warning above 190 MPH
why: POH 2-5: a micro switch in the throttle quadrant sounds the gear horn with the gear up and MP below 14 inches on either or both engines, so expect it whenever a throttle is pulled back.

q: With the gear up, the Seneca I gear warning horn sounds when manifold pressure drops below what value on either engine?
a: 14 in Hg
d: 12 in Hg
15 in Hg
18 in Hg
why: POH 2-5: gear up and MP reduced below 14 inches on one or both engines. The other horn condition is the gear selector in UP while on the ground.

q: N887SP is serial number 34-7350124. When the gear warning horn sounds in flight, what else should you see?
a: The red gear light illuminates with the horn
d: All three green lights flash
Nothing; the red light shows only in transit
The overvoltage light illuminates
why: POH 3-9: on serial numbers 34-7250046 and up, the red gear unsafe light also illuminates when the gear warning horn sounds. N887SP's serial is above that.

q: After retraction the red gear light stays illuminated. What does the POH say to do?
a: Recycle the landing gear
d: Pull the emergency gear extension knob
Pull the gear pump circuit breaker
Ignore it; it stays on for 30 seconds
why: POH 3-14: the red light shows the gear in transition between full up and down-and-locked; if it stays on, recycle the gear. It is off when the gear is fully up or fully down.

q: Where is the Seneca I landing gear safety (squat) switch, and what does it do?
a: Left main gear; keeps the pump from retracting on the ground
d: Nose gear strut; keeps the pump from retracting on the ground
Right main gear; silences the gear warning horn on the ground
Left main gear; mechanically locks the gear selector in DOWN
why: POH 2-6: with the selector UP on the ground, a safety switch on the left main gear prevents the hydraulic pump from running if the master switch is turned on.

q: On takeoff, how far must the oleo extend before the safety switch lets the pump retract the gear?
a: More than 8 inches
d: More than 2.5 inches
More than 3.5 inches
More than 12 inches
why: POH 2-6: when the oleo extends in excess of eight inches, the safety switch closes the circuit so the pump can raise the gear. 3.5 and 2.5 in are the static main and nose strut extensions.

q: Parked, a passenger bumps the gear selector to UP, and then you turn the master switch on. What happens?
a: The pump won't run, but the gear warning horn sounds
d: The gear begins retracting until the squat switch cuts the pump
Nothing happens; the warning horn works only in flight
The pump runs, but the downlocks hold the gear
why: POH 2-5/2-6: the left-main safety switch keeps the pump from actuating on the ground, and the horn sounds with the selector UP on the ground. Put the selector back to DOWN.

q: What are the Seneca I landing gear operating speed limits per POH 2-6?
a: Retract at up to 125 MPH; extend at up to 150 MPH
d: Retract or extend at up to 125 MPH
Retract at up to 150 MPH; extend at up to 125 MPH
Retract or extend at up to 150 MPH
why: POH 2-6: retract before 125 MPH is exceeded; extend at any speed up to 150 MPH. The selector placards read UP 125 MPH MAX and DOWN 150 MPH MAX.

q: How is the Seneca I steered on the ground, and through what arc?
a: Rudder pedals steer the nose gear through a 42° arc
d: Differential braking only; the nose wheel casters
Rudder pedals steer the nose gear through a 30° arc
A tiller steers the nose gear through a 60° arc
why: POH 2-6: the nose gear is steerable through a 42-degree arc with the rudder pedals. On retraction the linkage disengages and the wheel straightens; a centering spring prevents shimmy.

q: A line technician will tow the Seneca with a powered tug. How far may the nose gear be turned?
a: No more than 20° either side of center
d: No more than 42° either side of center
No more than 30° either side of center
No more than 10° either side of center
why: POH 9-1 caution: turning more than 20° either way with power equipment damages the nose gear and steering mechanism. 42° is the rudder-pedal steering arc.

q: Where is the Seneca I landing gear hydraulic reservoir?
a: Built into the pump, reached through the nose baggage area
d: Behind the rear baggage bulkhead, reached from the cabin
On the left firewall, reached through the cowl side panel
Shared with the brake reservoir in the nose compartment
why: POH 2-6: the reservoir is an integral part of the gear hydraulic pump, accessed through a panel in the nose baggage compartment. The brake reservoir is a separate unit.

q: The gear cycles normally, but the brakes feel spongy. Could the gear hydraulic system be the cause?
a: No; the brakes have their own independent reservoir
d: Yes; both systems draw on the gear pump's reservoir
Yes; the gear pump also pressurizes the brake lines
No; the brakes are mechanical, worked by cables
why: POH 2-6: the brake reservoir is independent of the gear reservoir and sits behind a panel at the rear top of the nose baggage compartment. Keep it at the marked level.

q: The brake reservoir needs topping off. What fluid does the POH specify?
a: MIL-H-5606 petroleum-base hydraulic fluid
d: MIL-H-83282 synthetic-base hydraulic fluid
Skydrol phosphate-ester hydraulic fluid
DOT 3 glycol-base automotive brake fluid
why: POH 9-6: the brake system is filled with MIL-H-5606 (petroleum base) fluid, checked periodically or at every 100-hour inspection.

q: Describe the Seneca I brake assemblies.
a: A single-disc, double-puck brake on each main gear
d: A dual-disc, single-puck brake on each main gear
Single-disc brakes on all three wheels
A drum brake on each main gear
why: POH 2-6: each main gear strut has a single-disc double-puck brake, actuated by toe brake cylinders and a hand-brake cylinder.

q: On the Seneca I, where are the toe brakes and the hand brake handle?
a: Left pedals (right optional); handle below left center panel
d: Both pedal sets standard; handle on the center floor console
Right pedals only; handle below the right side of the panel
Left pedals (right optional); handle on the tunnel by the flap lever
why: POH 2-6: toe brake cylinders are on the left rudder pedals (optional on the right), plus a handle-operated cylinder below and behind the left center of the instrument panel.

q: How is the Seneca I parking brake set and released?
a: Set: pull handle, push button. Release: pull handle only
d: Set: push button, pull handle. Release: push button again
Set: pull handle, turn it 90°. Release: turn it back and push
Set: press toe brakes, pull knob. Release: push knob
why: POH 2-6: pull back on the handle and push forward on the button to its left to set. To release, pull aft on the handle without touching the button and let it swing forward.

q: What tires does the Seneca I use?
a: 6.00-6 on all three; 6-ply nose, 8-ply mains
d: 6.00-6 on all three; 8-ply nose, 6-ply mains
5.00-5 6-ply nose; 6.00-6 8-ply mains
6.00-6 on all three; all 8-ply
why: POH 1-3 and 2-6: all three wheels are the same size, 6.00-6, with a six-ply nose tire and eight-ply main tires.

q: During preflight, what pressure should the Seneca I nose tire have?
a: 31 PSI
d: 53 PSI
42 PSI
25 PSI
why: POH 1-3 and 9-8 both give 31 PSI for the nose tire, and the school preflight checklist agrees. The main tires take 53 PSI (POH 9-8).

q: Per the POH Section 9 tire inflation guidance, what pressure should the main tires have?
a: 53 PSI
d: 31 PSI
42 PSI
60 PSI
why: POH 9-8 (servicing) and the school checklist give 53 PSI for the mains and 31 PSI for the nose. The Section 1 spec table (POH 1-3) prints 50 PSI for the mains; use the Section 9 servicing figure and confirm with your mechanic.

q: What type of shock struts does the Seneca I landing gear use?
a: Air-oil (oleo) struts on the nose and main gear
d: Spring-steel main legs with an air-oil nose strut
Rubber disc stacks on the nose and main gear
Air-oil main struts with a spring nose strut
why: POH 2-6: the nose and main gear struts are all air-oil assemblies. That is why the preflight checks exposed piston: 3-1/2 in on the mains, 2-1/2 in on the nose (POH 6-2, 9-6).

q: What circuit breakers protect the Seneca I landing gear system, per its electrical schematic?
a: 25-amp pump breaker; 5-amp control and warning breaker
d: One 25-amp breaker shared by the pump, lights and horn
15-amp pump breaker; 5-amp gear light and horn breaker
An in-line pump fuse; 10-amp control and warning breaker
why: The landing gear electrical schematic (POH 2-8) shows a 25-amp 'landing gear electro-hydraulic pump' breaker and a 5-amp 'landing gear control & warning' breaker.

q: On the Seneca I hydraulic schematic, what component does the emergency (free fall) control operate?
a: The free fall valve
d: The gear-up check valve in the pump
The high-pressure control valve
The shuttle valve below the reservoir
why: In the POH 2-7 schematic the free fall control is linked to the free fall valve. Opening it relieves the pressure holding the gear up so gravity, airloads and springs lower it.

q: Per the gear electrical schematic, what turns on each green gear light?
a: A down-limit switch at that gear
d: The hydraulic pressure switch
The squat switch on the left main gear
The throttle micro switch
why: The POH 2-8 schematic shows up-limit and down-limit switches at the left, nose and right gear, wired to their lights; POH 2-5 says three greens mean down and locked.

q: If the Seneca I hydraulic pump fails, is there any backup means of retracting the gear?
a: No; the backup only releases pressure so the gear falls
d: Yes; a hand pump on the floor beside the pilot's seat
Yes; pull the emergency knob out, then push it back in
Yes; airloads raise it once the emergency knob is pushed in
why: POH 2-5: the emergency system works only by relieving hydraulic pressure so the gear can free-fall. No manual retraction means is described; plan to fly with gear down.

q: After a hydraulic failure the gear has free-fallen and must stay down for a long leg. What speed change should you plan for?
a: True airspeed about 75% of the gear-up value
d: True airspeed about 90% of the gear-up value
True airspeed about 50% of the gear-up value
No change below 150 MPH
why: POH 6-9: with gear down, true airspeed is approximately 75% of the gear-retracted airspeed at the same power. Allow for the reduced speed and range.

q: What type of linkage connects the Seneca I cockpit controls to the flight control surfaces?
a: Cables
d: Push-pull tubes
Hydraulic actuators
Electric servos
why: POH 2-9: dual controls are standard, with a cable system between the controls and the surfaces.

q: How is pitch trim provided on the Seneca I?
a: Stabilator anti-servo tab, set from the control tunnel
d: Separate elevator trim tab, set by an overhead crank
Adjustable horizontal stabilizer, set by a jackscrew motor
Bungee springs on the control column, set by a panel knob
why: POH 2-9: the all-movable stabilator's anti-servo tab also acts as the longitudinal trim tab, worked by a control on the tunnel between the front seats. Your electric pitch trim drives the same trim, and the manual trim can overpower it (AFM electric trim supplement).

q: How does the Seneca I stabilator anti-servo tab move, and why?
a: Same direction as the stabilator, with more travel, for stability
d: Opposite the stabilator, like a servo tab, to reduce control forces
Same direction as the stabilator, but only when trim is moved
Opposite the stabilator, with more travel, to add pitch authority
why: POH 2-2: the tab moves in the same direction as the stabilator but with increased travel, which improves longitudinal stability (adds control feel) and provides trim.

q: What is the Seneca I rudder trim tab designed to do?
a: Relieve excessive pedal force in single-engine flight
d: Eliminate adverse yaw in normal coordinated turns
Hold the nose wheel straight for gear retraction
Counter P-factor during takeoff and climb power only
why: POH 2-2: the rudder trim tab can relieve the pilot of excessive pedal force during single-engine operation. Adverse yaw is handled by the aileron-rudder springs.

q: How does the Seneca I design reduce adverse yaw in turns?
a: Differential ailerons lightly spring-linked to the rudder
d: Frise-type ailerons combined with an electric yaw damper
Roll spoilers that deploy with each aileron input
A rudder trim tab geared to move with the ailerons
why: POH 2-9: the ailerons have differential action and are lightly interconnected with the rudder by springs, reducing adverse yaw and the coordination needed in normal turns.

q: What type of wing flaps does the Seneca I have?
a: Slotted
d: Split
Plain
Fowler
why: POH 2-1 describes slotted wing flaps, mechanically operated by a four-position handle between the front seats.

q: How are the Seneca I flaps moved, and what returns them to the retracted position?
a: A floor lever with a button; springs retract them
d: A panel switch and electric motor; the motor retracts them
The gear hydraulic pump; a relief valve retracts them
A floor lever with a button; only airloads retract them
why: POH 2-9: the flaps are extended manually by the lever on the floor between the front seats (depress the button on its end first). They are aerodynamically balanced for light forces and spring-loaded to return to retracted.

q: What flap settings are available on the Seneca I?
why: POH 2-9: three extended positions, 10, 25 and 40 degrees, plus retracted, matching the four-position handle in POH 2-1.

q: You've lost all electrical power on approach. Can you still extend the Seneca I flaps?
a: Yes; the flaps are fully manual, with no motor
d: No; the flap motor needs bus power
Only to 10°, using the emergency knob
Only if the hydraulic pump still has pressure
why: POH 2-9: the flaps are extended manually by a lever, so there is no flap motor. The gear, by contrast, would need the emergency free-fall knob.

q: Passengers are about to board and the flaps are at 10°. What does the POH recommend?
a: Retract fully; the right flap holds a step only when up
d: Leave them at 10° so the step up onto the wing is lower
Lower them to 40° so passengers clear the wing walk
Retract them; either flap can then be used as a boarding step
why: POH 2-9: a past-center lock holds the flap retracted so it can be used as a step on the right side. It won't support a step load unless fully retracted.

q: To what limit positive load factor was the Seneca I airframe designed and tested?
a: 3.8 g; aerobatics prohibited
d: 4.4 g; limited aerobatics allowed
6.0 g; aerobatics prohibited
3.8 g; spins approved with flaps up
why: POH 2-1: limit positive load factor 3.8; the Seneca is not designed for aerobatic flight, so aerobatics are prohibited. The limitations repeat 3.8 g flaps up.

q: What are the Seneca I wing span and wing area?
a: 38.88 ft span; 208.7 sq ft area
d: 38.88 ft span; 178.0 sq ft area
28.5 ft span; 208.7 sq ft area
42.0 ft span; 208.7 sq ft area
why: POH 1-2: span 38.88 ft, area 208.7 sq ft, length 28.5 ft, height 9.9 ft, wing loading 20.1 lb/sq ft and power loading 10.5 lb/hp. Wheel base is 7.0 ft and tread 11.1 ft (POH 1-3).

q: How many fuel tanks does the Seneca I have, and how are they arranged?
a: Four: two interconnected 24.5-gal tanks per wing
d: Two: one 49-gal tank in each wing
Four: main and auxiliary tanks selected separately
Six: three interconnected tanks per wing
why: POH 2-10: two 24.5-gallon aluminum tanks in each wing are interconnected, so each wing works as one tank for selection (POH 3-8). Both fill through one neck in the outboard tank, and outboard fuel flows inboard as it is used.

q: What is the Seneca I total fuel capacity, and how much of it is unusable?
a: 98 gal total; 5 gal unusable (2.5 per side)
d: 98 gal total; 2.5 gal unusable in all
93 gal total; 5 gal unusable (2.5 per side)
100 gal total; 7 gal unusable (3.5 per side)
why: POH 1-2 and 2-10: 98 gallons total (49 per wing, POH 9-7) with 2-1/2 unusable gallons per side, leaving 93 gallons usable.

q: You have the tanks topped off to the bottom of the filler necks. How much usable fuel is on each side?
a: 46.5 gal
d: 49 gal
47.5 gal
44 gal
why: Each wing holds 49 gal (POH 9-7) less 2.5 gal unusable (POH 2-10) = 46.5 gal, the usable capacity on the filler cap placard (POH 3-5).

q: What fuel does the Seneca I POH require?
a: 100/130 octane minimum aviation gasoline
d: 80/87 octane minimum aviation gasoline
91/96 octane minimum aviation gasoline
Jet A or 100/130 aviation gasoline
why: POH 1-2, 2-10 and 3-1 require 100/130 minimum; the POH lists no lower alternate grade. POH 9-7 warns lower grades can quickly cause serious damage and void the engine warranty.

q: How many fuel pumps does the Seneca I fuel system have?
a: Four: an engine-driven and an electric pump per engine
d: Two: one engine-driven pump per engine and no electric pumps
Three: two engine-driven pumps and one shared electric pump
Two: one electric pump in each wing, no engine-driven pumps
why: POH 2-10: each engine has an engine-driven pump as the primary supply and an electric pump as a backup in case the engine-driven pump fails.

q: Where are the Seneca I electric (auxiliary) fuel pumps located?
a: On the aft side of each firewall
d: Inside each inboard fuel tank
Under the cabin floor by the selectors
On the forward side of each firewall
why: POH 2-10: an electric pump on the aft side of the firewall for each engine. POH 9-7 puts the gascolators between the selector valves and these boost pumps in the nacelles.

q: When does the POH say to use the electric fuel pumps?
a: Takeoff and landing, and if an engine-driven pump fails
d: Continuously above 10,000 ft to prevent fuel vapor lock
Only for engine starting and priming, then turned off
Whenever either fuel selector is placed on CROSSFEED
why: POH 2-10: the electric pumps back up the engine-driven pumps and should be on for takeoffs and landings in case an engine-driven pump fails then. The switches are on the panel left of the pilot.

q: Above 500 ft AGL after takeoff, what procedure does the POH give for turning off the electric fuel pumps?
a: One at a time, watching that fuel pressure stays green
d: Both at once, then verify fuel flow is equal
One at a time, watching that RPM stays constant
Both at once, after setting the cruise mixture
why: POH 6-8: the electric pumps may be turned off one at a time above 500 ft AGL, monitoring fuel pressure to see it stays in the green. The school climb checklist matches.

q: Where are the Seneca I fuel selectors, and what positions do they have?
a: On the tunnel between the front seats: OFF, ON, CROSSFEED
d: On the floor between the seats: LEFT, RIGHT, BOTH, OFF
On the left sidewall below the panel: ON, OFF, CROSSFEED
On the overhead panel: MAIN, AUXILIARY, CROSSFEED, OFF
why: POH 2-10: the selectors are on the tunnel between the pilot and copilot seats, and each lever has OFF, ON and CROSSFEED. Normally each engine draws from its own wing.

q: What two purposes does the POH give for the Seneca I crossfeed?
a: Extend single-engine range and keep fuel weight balanced
d: Feed both engines in an emergency and aid engine priming
Transfer fuel between the wing tanks and drain water
Supply the cabin heater and balance fuel while on the ground
why: POH 2-10: the crossfeed lines let an engine use fuel from the opposite side, to extend single-engine range and to keep the fuel weight balanced.

q: Left engine feathered, you are cruising level on the right engine and want to use left-wing fuel. How should the selectors be set?
a: Right selector CROSSFEED; left selector OFF
d: Left selector CROSSFEED; right selector ON
Both selectors on CROSSFEED
Right selector ON; left selector CROSSFEED
why: POH 3-8: put the operating engine's selector on CROSSFEED and the inoperative engine's OFF, electric pumps off unless an engine-driven pump has failed. Use crossfeed in level flight only.

q: After crossfeeding during single-engine cruise, how should the fuel selectors be set before landing?
a: Operating engine ON (its own side); inoperative engine OFF
d: Operating engine stays on CROSSFEED; inoperative OFF
Both selectors ON
Operating engine CROSSFEED; inoperative engine ON
why: POH 2-10: before landing, select fuel from the same side as the operating engine. POH 3-9 adds the operating engine's electric pump ON for landing.

q: What two crossfeed restrictions are stated in the NOTE on POH 2-10?
a: Never both selectors on CROSSFEED; no takeoff on CROSSFEED
d: Never both on CROSSFEED; no crossfeed above 10,000 ft
No takeoff on CROSSFEED; no crossfeed with pumps off
No crossfeed with both engines running; no landing on ON
why: POH 2-10 NOTE: do not operate with both fuel selectors on CROSSFEED, and do not take off with a selector on CROSSFEED. Section 3 also limits crossfeed to level flight.

q: Both engines running in cruise, the left wing has 10 gal more than the right. How can you rebalance using the POH fuel system?
a: Right selector to CROSSFEED, left stays ON, until even
d: Left selector to CROSSFEED, right stays ON, until even
Both selectors to CROSSFEED until even
Both electric pumps on to transfer fuel across
why: POH 3-9 permits running both engines from the same tank in cruise. With the right selector on CROSSFEED, both engines draw from the left wing until the sides even up; never put both selectors on CROSSFEED (POH 2-10).

q: With one engine inoperative, can the operating engine use the fuel in both wings?
a: Yes, by moving its selector between ON and CROSSFEED
d: No; each wing can feed only its own engine
Yes, but only with both selectors on CROSSFEED
Yes, by running both electric pumps to transfer it
why: POH 2-10/3-8: crossfeed lets an engine use the opposite wing's fuel, so the good engine can use both sides (less 2.5 gal unusable per side). Both selectors on CROSSFEED is prohibited.

q: How is fuel quantity measured and displayed in the Seneca I?
a: A sender in each tank; one gauge shows each wing's total
d: One sender per wing; a separate cockpit gauge for each tank
Sight gauges in each tank, read on preflight
A digital totalizer that computes quantity from fuel flow
why: POH 2-10: a sender in each of the four tanks electrically transmits the total in each pair of tanks to a single gauge per wing; fuel pressure and fuel flow gauges are also provided.

q: Where in the fuel flow path is each Seneca I gascolator (fuel filter) located?
a: Between the fuel selector valve and the electric fuel pump
d: Between the engine-driven fuel pump and the fuel injector servo
Inside each inboard tank, at the fuel outlet
Between the flow divider and the injector nozzles
why: POH 2-10: one gascolator per side between the selector valve and the electric pump. Its drain is on the inboard side of the nacelle, forward of and below the wing leading edge.

q: How many fuel quick drains does the Seneca I have in total, and what are they?
a: Eight: 4 tank, 2 gascolator, 2 crossfeed
d: Six: 4 tank, 2 gascolator
Eight: 4 tank, 2 gascolator, 2 fuel injector
Ten: 4 tank, 2 gascolator, 4 crossfeed
why: POH 2-10: quick drains for each fuel tank (4), the fuel gascolators (2) and each crossfeed line (2).

q: Where are the Seneca I fuel crossfeed line drains?
a: Under the belly, opposite the right flap trailing edge
d: Under the belly, opposite the left flap trailing edge
Under each nacelle, next to the gascolator drain
Under each wing, just outboard of the tank drains
why: POH 2-10 puts the two crossfeed drains under the fuselage opposite the trailing edge of the right flap (POH 9-7: inboard of the right flap). They are drained on the right-side walk-around (POH 6-2).

q: What makes up the Seneca I fuel tank vent system?
a: Cap vents, a vent link between tanks, filler-neck overflows
d: A single NACA vent under each wingtip and nothing else
Cap vents only, since the tanks in each wing are not interconnected
Cap vents plus a vent line routed to the heater fuel pump
why: POH 2-10: a vent in each fuel cap, a vent interconnect between the tanks in each wing, and an overflow line from the top of each filler neck. Check the cap vent on preflight (POH 6-2).

q: Using the POH fuel schematic, what is the order of components from the tanks to the cylinders?
a: Selector, filter, electric pump, engine pump, injector, divider
d: Filter, selector, engine pump, electric pump, injector, divider
Selector, electric pump, filter, injector, engine pump, divider
Selector, filter, engine pump, divider, injector, electric pump
why: POH 2-11 schematic and 2-10 text: selector valve, gascolator (filter), electric pump, engine-driven pump, fuel injector (servo), then the flow divider and nozzles.

q: What are the Seneca I fuel pressure green arc and fuel flow red line?
a: 14–35 PSI green; 19.2 GPH fuel flow red line
d: 14–35 PSI green; 20.6 GPH fuel flow red line
25–60 PSI green; 19.2 GPH fuel flow red line
5–15 PSI green; 10.3 GPH fuel flow red line
why: POH 3-2: fuel pressure green 14–35 PSI with red lines at 14 (minimum) and 35 (maximum); fuel flow red line 19.2 GPH. 20.6 GPH is total two-engine burn at 75% power.

q: In cruise, one fuel flow gauge reads noticeably higher than the other and more than you are actually burning. What does the POH suggest?
a: A clogged fuel nozzle on that engine
d: A failed engine-driven fuel pump
A selector partly on CROSSFEED
A blocked fuel cap vent
why: POH 6-9: a fuel flow reading well above actual consumption, or an asymmetric flow indication, may mean a clogged fuel nozzle that should be cleaned. Cross-check time, power and fuel used.

q: How are the Seneca I engines primed for a normal start?
a: Electric pump on; mixture rich until fuel flow shows, then cutoff
d: Panel plunger primer, three strokes, with mixture at cutoff
Pump the throttle three times with the mixture full rich
Hold the electric primer button for 3 seconds per engine
why: POH 6-3: with the electric fuel pumps on, move the mixture to rich until fuel flow is indicated and stabilized, then back to idle cut-off. Hot starts skip priming (pumps off).

q: In cruise, with plenty of fuel in the right tanks, the right engine's fuel pressure drops and the engine starts to falter. What backup does the fuel system provide?
a: Turn on the right electric fuel pump
d: Move the right selector to CROSSFEED
Pull the right alternate air control
Feather the right engine at once
why: POH 2-10: each engine's electric pump is the backup for its engine-driven pump (POH 3-8 repeats this). Crossfeed changes the fuel source, not the pump, so it would not cure a failed engine-driven pump.

q: Why does the POH caution against a fast taxi turn onto the runway and immediate takeoff without the electric pumps on?
a: It can cause temporary malfunction of one engine
d: It can overheat and fade the brakes
It can open the squat switch and retract the gear
It can shift the CG beyond the aft limit
why: POH 3-9: fast taxi turns right before the takeoff run can cause temporary malfunction of one engine if the electric boost pumps are not ON. POH 6-7 adds the warning about low fuel.

q: What supplies the varying oil pressure that each Seneca I propeller uses to hold the selected RPM?
a: An engine-mounted governor, through the propeller shaft
d: The engine oil pump, through a fixed pressure regulator
An electric pump in each nacelle, set by the prop lever
The nitrogen charge in the dome, through a regulator
why: POH 2-4: a governor on each engine supplies oil through the propeller shaft at varying pressures to keep a constant RPM. Oil pressure moves the blades toward high RPM; the dome's nitrogen charge pushes them toward feather.

q: Why does the POH call for smooth, not-too-rapid throttle movements on the Seneca I engines?
a: To avoid engine wear and damage to the dynamic counterweights
d: To avoid flooding the float carburetors and fouling the plugs
To keep the fuel injection servo from vapor locking at idle
To protect the alternators and regulators from sudden voltage surges
why: POH 2-3: smooth throttle operation prevents unnecessary engine wear and damage to the engines' dynamic counterweights. The engines are fuel injected, so there are no carburetors to flood.

q: Which way does the Seneca I nose gear retract, and how does that help a free-fall extension?
a: Forward; once it starts down, the airstream pushes it to lock
d: Aft; the springs must overcome the airstream to lock it down fully
Inboard; gravity alone swings it down and into the locks
Aft; the airstream then pushes it down and into the downlock
why: POH 2-5: the mains fold inboard toward the centerline and the nose gear retracts forward. Once the nose gear starts down, the airstream pushes on it and helps it lock, along with gravity and springs.

q: Where are the Seneca I's standard cabin entry doors?
a: A front door on the right and a rear door on the left
d: A front door on the left and a rear door on the right
Front and rear doors, both on the right side
Front and rear doors, both on the left side
why: POH 2-1: the fuselage has a front door on the right side and a rear door on the left; a large rear cargo door is available as an option. The right flap can be used as a step only when fully retracted (POH 2-9).
